claims.text: An equiatomic five-component HfNbTaTiZr alloy has maximized configurational entropy for that set of components.
High configurational entropy favors stabilization of a single-phase BCC solid solution in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Dissolved oxygen stabilizes an alpha-HCP phase in HfNbTaTiZr.
Zr or Ti getters react with residual oxygen to form stable ZrO2 or TiO2 and thereby prevent oxygen dissolution in the alloy.
Zirconium is the most chemically compatible getter because it is an alloy constituent, forms stable ZrO2, and its excess can be managed.
TaH0.5 decomposes at approximately 400–500 °C.
NbH decomposes at approximately 300–400 °C.
HfH2 decomposes at approximately 600–700 °C.
TiH2 decomposes at approximately 400–500 °C.
ZrH2 decomposes at approximately 300–400 °C.
Heating at 10–20 °C/min, sintering at 900–1000 °C, homogenizing at 1100–1200 °C, and quenching faster than 100 K/s are required to trap beta-BCC HfNbTaTiZr.
An argon atmosphere containing less than 10 ppm oxygen is suitable for processing the alloy.
A getter addition of 2–5 wt% excess relative to theoretical oxygen uptake is sufficient for oxygen control.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion-controlled phase separation and alpha-HCP nucleation.
Rapid quenching will yield metastable single-phase beta-BCC HfNbTaTiZr.
The quenched alloy will have a grain size of 1–5 micrometers.
The proposed process will produce a nearly fully dense alloy with less than 2% porosity.
No alpha-HCP or alpha-Ti phase will be detected after rapid quenching.
The resulting alloy will have a hardness of approximately 400–500 HV and good ductility because of its single-phase BCC structure.
Sequential hydride decomposition enables uniform alloying without high-energy ball milling and consequently reduces contamination.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis first calls Ti or Zr powder unsuitable because they are alloy constituents, but subsequently selects Zr or Ti as the preferred getter and includes them in the feedstock.

The target and predicted product are described as equiatomic, while adding 2–5 wt% excess Zr or Ti directly to the blend would alter the equiatomic composition unless the getter is physically separated.
The intervention assigns sequential decomposition to 400–800 °C, whereas the hypothesis assigns NbH and ZrH2 decomposition ranges beginning at 300 °C.

The 1–5 micrometer grain-size prediction is attributed partly to rapid solidification, but the proposed route is solid-state sintering and homogenization below the stated melting point, with no melting or solidification step identified.

The experiment measures phases throughout heating, but the falsification rule only treats alpha-HCP during cooling or in the final microstructure as falsifying; it does not make alpha-HCP during the critical hydride-decomposition window decisive.
